image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / waffle-style dot matrix chart** showing percentages as a 10×10 grid of circles.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **100-unit grid** (small repeated marks) to represent proportions.
   - Categories are distinguished by **different fill/outline styles** rather than separate panels.
   - Includes **leader lines/arrows** connecting the text list of categories to corresponding rows/segments in the dot grid.
   - No faceting or stacking in the usual bar/area sense.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Skill option / category (e.g., Three languages of your choice, Chef skills, Neuroscience, Oil painting, Repairing any home appliance, Gymnastics) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels in the left annotation box; differentiated in the dot grid by fill/outline style and linked with leader lines/arrows |
| Percentage / share (%) | Quantitative | Number of circles occupied in the 10×10 grid; also shown as text percentages in the label box |
| Unit count out of 100 | Quantitative | Repeated circle marks in the grid (each circle representing one unit/percent) |
| Grid position | Ordinal/layout | Position of circles in rows and columns within the matrix to accumulate the total percentages |

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of people would prefer to master skills that they thought would help them be more successful in life, whether it be through being able to communicate with more people (as shown by those who selected being able to speak three languages) or being able to cook for themselves. Far fewer individuals were interested in more creative skills, such as oil painting and gymnastics, hinting that they do not believe there is much to be gained from knowing how to do either of these activities. There does seem to be an overwhelming favor of more "white collar," higher paying jobs, as language fluency and neuroscience would both lead to higher salaries.

I wonder why these were the options. Oil painting seems like a very specific activity, compared to maybe just asking the students if they would want to master just painting. Also, I am curious to see if the students were searching for the "correct" answer or if maybe there was a bias in the polling, as different nationalities or classes might prioritize different skills. As those who participated were subscribers to the New York Times, they might be more interested in more academic activities verses those relating to art, physical education, or home maintenance.

These graph shows what skills high schoolers value, hinting on what classes they will take, degrees they will obtain, and eventually what the job market and the workforce will look like.

"A White Collar Future: America's Upcoming Workforce."

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that the majority of those that opted into the survey, 60%, said that they would instantly master three languages of their choice. Directly right after follows 12% of people who said that they would prefer mastering chef skills, and then 11% with neuroscience mastery. 
2. I wonder as to why the gap between mastering three languages and the rest of the skills varies by such a large amount. The difference between 60% and 12% is 48%. I think that this could be because people are just generally interested in immersing themselves in a rich culture that is not their own. Language is the key to understanding people who do not look like you, and great for making connections between one another. 
3. The impact that this would have is having a greater understanding and appreciation for the different cultures that exist in my community. I think that it is so important to understand at least another language because English is not the only language out there with a large amount of speakers.  It would be great to fully understand our differences and how we can make each other smile with the words that we can speak. 
4. In this graph, we get to see the percentages of people who selected a specific skill to instantly master. Catchy headline: "US Priority: To Cook or to Speak?"

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs).

Keep noticing and wondering.  This is the last graph of 2020.  The next graph release will be by Friday, Jan. 1, 2021 with moderation on Wednesday, Jan. 6.  Stay tuned for which graph will be posted.

comments.raw_comment: I think it is important to point out that the survey only provided a few options for skills. Of course, giving people completing the survey unlimited options for possible skills would make it difficult to organize responses in a meaningful way, it should be recognized that changing the options for skills could drastically affect the results of the survey. I notice that many of the skills all require a significant time commitment. I wonder if perhaps the survey takers chose the skills because of the time investment they would require. I also wonder if the skills chosen reflect how the survey takers spend their free time (those who chose chef skills having an interest in baking, for example.) This graph could affect my community by showing what skills those in my community will be most likely to invest time in (though of course the results would be more accurate to my community if the survey was conducted entirely inside of it.) If I were to create a headline for this graphic, I would make it say "The Skills People Want."
